verse.text: O give thanks unto the LORD, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
verse.summary: Psalm 107 opens a long song sung by the redeemed — wanderers in the desert, prisoners in chains, the sick at death's door, sailors at their wits' end — and every one of them cried unto the LORD in their trouble and was delivered. Over and over the psalm sighs the same wish: "Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness." It's the same thing Jesus looked for on a Samaritan road, when ten lepers were cleansed and only one came back to say thank you. Before you ask God for one more thing today, go back and thank Him for the last thing — His goodness is not a mood, and His mercy has no expiry date.

sermon.title: Where Are the Nine?
sermon.excerpt: Ten lepers cried for mercy, and all ten were cleansed on the road. Only one turned back to fall at Jesus' feet — and Jesus asked a question that still stings: were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?

bibleStudy.title: Doest Thou Well to Be Angry?

verses.text: Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me. But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.

And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not. But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil. Therefore now, O LORD, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live. Then said the LORD, Doest thou well to be angry?

And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd. But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered. And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said, It is better for me to die than to live. And God said to Jonah, Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd? And he said, I do well to be angry, even unto death. Then said the LORD, Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?

bibleStudy.excerpt: Jonah survived a storm, three days inside a fish, and the single biggest revival in the Old Testament — and the only thing that nearly broke him was watching God be merciful to people he'd already decided didn't deserve it.
body: Everybody thinks the book of Jonah is a fish story. It isn't. The fish is the most obedient character in the entire book — it goes exactly where it's sent, holds exactly as long as it's told, and lets go right on schedule. If you want the actual antagonist of Jonah, stop looking in the water and look at the man sitting on a hillside outside Nineveh a few chapters later, sulking under a dying plant because God had just been too merciful to people Jonah had already decided didn't deserve it. That's the real plot of this book. The storm, the lots, the sailors, the three days in the dark — all of it is just the detour God took to drag a reluctant prophet to the sermon that actually mattered, and that sermon was never for Nineveh. It was for Jonah. Honestly, it still is, for a lot of us.

Start where the book starts, because the opening verse already tells you everything you need to know about the man you're dealing with. "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me." One sentence. One assignment. Nothing vague about it. And Jonah's response isn't confusion, isn't a request for clarification, isn't even an argument on the spot — "But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD." Look at the geography for a second, because it's doing more work than it looks like: Nineveh was east, near modern-day Mosul in Iraq. Tarshish was almost certainly west, out past Gibraltar — the furthest point on the known map in the opposite direction a man could physically buy passage to. Jonah didn't take a scenic detour. He purchased the maximum available planet between himself and one city. And notice this isn't a coward's flight — this same man will later stand alone in the middle of a hostile capital and preach judgment to its face with nothing but his own voice. Jonah wasn't afraid of Nineveh. Jonah was afraid of what God might do for Nineveh, and we find out exactly why two chapters from now, straight from his own mouth.

Skip the storm, skip the lots the sailors cast, skip the three days in the fish's belly — not because they don't matter, but because all they actually change is Jonah's longitude, not his heart. The prayer he prays in the fish is desperate, not repentant, and you can tell, because the moment he's back on dry land God gives him the exact same assignment, word for word, like a teacher handing a student the homework he tried to skip. This time Jonah goes. He walks into the city and preaches eight words in the Hebrew — the shortest, least enthusiastic sermon in the whole of Scripture, no altar call, no invitation, not even a mention of mercy — and the entire city, from the king on his throne down to the livestock in the field, repents in sackcloth and ashes before he's even finished clearing his throat. "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not." Read that as what it is: the single largest, fastest, most complete revival recorded anywhere in the Old Testament, bigger than anything Elijah or Elisha ever witnessed, produced by a prophet who didn't even want the job. The fish obeyed the first time it was told. It took Jonah two tries. And he's still the one we remember as the reluctant one, which tells you something about how low the bar for obedience actually is.

Now watch what the most statistically successful preacher in the Old Testament does the moment his sermon works, because this is where the book stops being a children's story and starts being a mirror you don't especially want held up. "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." Not mildly disappointed — exceedingly displeased. The revival of a lifetime, the kind of result most preachers would trade their whole ministry for, and Jonah is furious about it. Then listen to what he actually prays, because it might be the strangest prayer in the entire Bible — he doesn't confess, he doesn't give thanks, he files a complaint: "I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil." Read that confession again slowly, because Jonah just told God, two chapters later, the real reason he ran from Nineveh back in chapter one — and it wasn't fear of the Assyrians. It was theology. Jonah knew exactly who God was: gracious, merciful, slow to anger. He loved every one of those attributes when they covered his own disobedience in the belly of a fish. He hated every one of them the moment they might cover his enemies in the streets of their own city.

And God's response to all that fury is not a lecture. It's a question — four words that are going to come back twice before this book is finished: "Doest thou well to be angry?" No rebuke, no argument, just a question Jonah refuses to answer, and his silence is itself an answer. He storms out of the city, builds himself a booth on the east side, and sits down to watch — presumably still hoping God will torch Nineveh on a technicality, forty days not being quite up yet. Here's my real question for you today, and I need you to actually sit in it instead of reading past it toward the gourd: has somebody else's forgiveness ever genuinely offended you? Not their sin — their forgiveness. The relative who got the apology you never got. The coworker who got the second chance you weren't given. The person your heart has already sentenced, who then goes and gets mercy from God anyway, mercy that costs you nothing and still somehow manages to make you furious. If that's never happened to you, you've never really understood grace. Mercy toward you feels like relief. Mercy toward your enemy feels, if you're honest, like an injustice done to you personally — and that feeling is exactly what had Jonah sitting in a self-built booth, sulking at the edge of the very revival he'd just produced.

So God, with what I can only describe as a sense of humor sharp enough to double as surgery, prepares a plant to grow up over Jonah's booth, "that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief." Jonah is "exceeding glad of the gourd" — the first unqualified joy recorded anywhere in this whole book, and it's over a houseplant. Then, right on schedule, God prepares a worm to kill it overnight and a scorching east wind to finish the job by morning, and Jonah — a man who has already survived a shipwreck, a storm, and three days inside a fish — is now ready to die over a wilted vine. "It is better for me to die than to live," he says, for the second time in two chapters, and both times it's over something that cost him nothing and belonged to him for less than a day. God asks him again, this time naming the object plainly: "Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?" And Jonah, somehow still missing the whole point of his own book, doubles down: "I do well to be angry, even unto death." Then comes the line that should end every sermon on comfortable religion for the rest of church history: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: and should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" Jonah grieved a plant he didn't plant, didn't water, and didn't own, for exactly one day — and resented God for sparing a hundred and twenty thousand image-bearers. That's not an ancient problem. That's Tuesday for most of us: more compassion for our own comfort than for people we've already decided don't count.

Here's my real question for you today, and this time I actually want you to name it, not just nod at it: who is your Nineveh? Who is the person, the family, the political tribe, the whole category of people that, if you heard God had forgiven them completely, wiped the slate, blessed their house, answered their prayer — your honest first reaction wouldn't be joy, it would be something closer to outrage? Maybe it's the parent who hurt you and never apologized and somehow still prospers. Maybe it's a whole group of people your community taught you to write off before you ever met one of them personally. Maybe it's simpler and more private than either of those — somebody who wronged you specifically, by name, and you have quietly, respectably, been hoping God takes His time with them. Jonah's problem was never a lack of theology. He had better theology than most of us — he could quote God's own attributes back to Him word for word. His problem was that he didn't actually want those attributes to apply past the border of his own comfort.

And here's the detail that should unsettle you the most, because this book does something almost no other book in Scripture does: it ends on a question, and Jonah never answers it. God asks, "should not I spare Nineveh, that great city," and the text simply stops. No recorded reply. No note on whether Jonah repented of his anger, forgave the city, came down off the hillside, or just sat there resentful until the sun went down on him too. The author leaves it open on purpose, because the real audience of that final question was never just one sulking prophet on a hill outside an ancient capital — it's everybody who's ever read this book since, including you, today, with whatever Nineveh you've been quietly hoping God would judge a little harder and a little slower than He judged you. So let me put God's own question to you the way He left it hanging over Jonah: doest thou well to be angry? Is your fury at somebody else's mercy actually righteous, or is it just old pride wearing theology as a disguise? Come down off the hillside. Let the gourd die if it has to die. Let God be as gracious to your Nineveh as He already was to you in your own fish, your own storm, your own flight in the opposite direction — because if He'd kept score on you the way you're keeping it on them, neither one of you would still be standing here. Answer the question He never got an answer to. Go and love what He loves, even the people it costs you something to forgive. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that I am not one of the nine — I see what You have done, and I am coming back to say thank You!
I will not be loud in my trouble and silent in my blessing!
With a loud voice I glorify God, and I fall at the feet of Jesus!
I was healed on the way — so I keep walking even before I see it!
What You did for me will never become just normal to me!
I forget not all His benefits — He forgiveth all my iniquities, He healeth all my diseases!
I am not only cleansed — my faith has made me whole!
My gratitude is a door, not a goodbye — I go from the miracle to the Master!
O give thanks unto the LORD, for He is good: His mercy endureth for ever!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. We are the one who came back — and we are made whole! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: Not One Evil Deposit Remains
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not about any one dream scene — it meets every attempt in the dream realm to plant, inject, transplant, or deposit anything foreign into your body, blood, organs, or spirit while you sleep, however it was delivered: a touch, a handshake, a meal at a strange table, an object pressed into your hand or skin. Whatever the vessel, nothing illegitimate stays in you. Pray this aloud before you close your eyes, in Jesus' name.
points: Father, Your Word declares in Matthew 15:13, "...Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up" — every evil seed, deposit, or foreign growth planted into my body, blood, or spirit through any dream contact tonight is uprooted now, root and branch, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the authority Christ gave me in Mark 16:18, "...they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them..." — every deadly substance, poison, or venom administered to me through food, drink, touch, or injection in a dream tonight is rendered powerless over my body, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, as in 2 Kings 4:41, "...Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot" — every poisoned meal, cup, or morsel served to me at any table in the dream realm tonight is purged, and there is no harm in my pot, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I stand on Job 33:24-25, "Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom... His flesh shall be fresher than a child's" — every foreign thing lodged in my flesh by a dream encounter is flushed out by the ransom of the blood, and my body returns fresher than a child's, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Your Word declares in Exodus 15:26, "...I will put none of these diseases upon thee...for I am the LORD that healeth thee" — no disease, affliction, or planted sickness assigned to my body through a dream tonight can stand, for You alone are the LORD that healeth me, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the pattern of Luke 13:16, "...whom Satan hath bound...be loosed from this bond..." — every bondage fastened to my body or organs while I slept, every chain tied around what was deposited in me, is loosed now, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, as in Isaiah 58:6, "...to loose the bands of wickedness...and that ye break every yoke" — every band of wickedness wrapped around my blood, my bones, or my breath in a dream tonight is loosed, and every yoke of foreign deposit is broken off me, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I decree by 1 Peter 2:24, "...by whose stripes ye were healed" — every wound, implant, or evil material forced into my body in the dream realm is answered by the stripes of Calvary; I am already healed, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Your Word declares in Leviticus 17:11, "For the life of the flesh is in the blood...for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul" — the blood of Jesus, not any foreign substance, is the life in my flesh tonight; every bloodline opened to receive an evil deposit is sealed shut, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the authority of Colossians 1:13, "Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son" — I am already removed from the territory where such deposits have power; darkness has no jurisdiction to plant anything in a citizen of the kingdom of light, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Your Word declares in Psalm 41:3, "The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness" — my bed is Yours tonight, not a laboratory for the enemy's experiments; every attack assigned to my sickbed in a dream is turned into a bed of strength, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I decree by Joel 2:25, "...I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten..." — whatever strength, health, or virtue any dream deposit has eaten from my body over time is restored to me in full tonight, in the mighty name of Jesus!

So I seal tonight with Revelation 12:11, "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony..." — by that same blood and that same word, I overcome every foreign deposit, every planted thing, every evil transplant assigned to my body and spirit while I slept. I wake in the morning whole, untouched, and Mine alone to the glory of God — in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
